outcome: As of 11 Oct 2026 the GRH is not settled: no accepted proof or disproof exists. Since 26 Jan 2024 the events are (i) unconditional lower bounds on the proportion of zeros that are simple and on the line, for each fixed primitive Dirichlet character (Alpöge and Furman, arXiv:2608.13637, Aug 2026, whose argument its authors credit to Claude) and for averaged families of characters (Hua and Yang, Aug 2026; Johns, Sep 2026); (ii) an OpenAI release of 6 Oct 2026 claiming a zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 for every Dirichlet L-function, plus a uniform gap for real zeros of real characters, neither peer reviewed; (iii) unrefereed claimed proofs of the GRH (Zhang 2025–26; Blinovsky, whose GRH claim was dropped in Dec 2025), and an earlier 2019 claimed proof (Agélas) whose key lemma Brent called false in 2021.
problem_asks: Whether every nontrivial zero of every Dirichlet L-function lies on the critical line, i.e. has the form 1/2 + it with real t. Unpacked: (1) the family: L(s,χ) for every Dirichlet character χ of every modulus q, including imprimitive characters, real (quadratic and other real-valued) characters, and the trivial character, whose L-function is ζ(s) up to finitely many Euler factors, so that its case is the Riemann hypothesis; (2) the objects: nontrivial zeros, meaning zeros with 0 < Re s < 1 (the trivial zeros at negative integers are not asked about); (3) the location claim: each such zero ρ has Re ρ = 1/2; (4) the answer is yes/no: yes if the claim holds for all χ, no if one nontrivial zero off the line exists for some χ. Not asked by the statement: multiplicity or simplicity of zeros, counts or proportions of zeros, zero-free regions short of the line, any restriction to primitive characters, bounded height, or averages over characters. The parent (grand RH) asks the same for all automorphic L-functions and is not part of this bullet.

events.what_happened: Anthropic blog post 'Claude has improved on a longstanding lower bound for the fraction of zeros of the Riemann zeta function that satisfy the Riemann hypothesis' (dated 10 Aug 2026, updated 13 Aug 2026), and arXiv:2608.13637 by Levent Alpöge and Ralph Furman, 'More than two thirds of the zeta zeros are simple and on the critical line' (v1 13 Aug 2026; v2 19 Aug 2026). The blog states the bound rose from 41.6% to 67.2% (zeros on the critical line). The arXiv abstract gives: at least two thirds of nontrivial zeta zeros, counted with multiplicity, are simple and on the line, and at least five sixths are distinct; with the Montgomery–Taylor window the constants are 0.6725 and 0.8362. Theorem B (§1.1, read in the HTML version): 'Theorem A holds verbatim for L(s,χ) in place of ζ(s), for any fixed primitive Dirichlet character χ.' The abstract says 'The results extend to primitive Dirichlet L-functions and are formally verified in Lean 4.' The main results are stated as unconditional, and §1.3 says RH 'entered only to read the zero side termwise'. §1.5 and the title footnote state the argument was produced by Claude.

The first full written argument is arXiv v1 on 13 Aug 2026; the judging pass may prefer that date.
events.delivers: For ζ(s): unconditional lower bounds of about 2/3 (0.6725 with the Montgomery–Taylor window) for the proportion of zeros in windows (T, 2T) that are simple and on Re s = 1/2, and 5/6 (0.8362) for distinct zeros. disputes.summary: Credit for the zeta bound of two-thirds simple zeros on the line (67.25%): the arXiv paper lists Alpöge and Furman as authors, with the comments and title footnote saying the argument was discovered by Claude. Anthropic's post says Claude found the argument and that Alpöge and Furman validated it. Lamzouri credits the bound to 'an internal research version of Claude' and then to Alpöge and Furman's verification. The Johns page attributes the constants to Alpöge and Furman. These readings are not reconciled in any source I read.

Two different Anthropic-linked figures are often merged: the blog's 41.6% → 67.2% concerns zeros on the critical line (no simple qualifier), whereas the arXiv headline (two thirds) concerns zeros that are simple and on the line, and its Theorem B concerns each fixed primitive Dirichlet character.

Which OpenAI family-003 paper states 7/8 and which 11/12: the repository index assigns 7/8 to the lead paper and 11/12 to the companion; a secondary summary says the repository's paper states 11/12. Also, the lead paper's abstract allows the principal pole at s = 1, while the Lean description excludes it.

Knausgård's title (more than 67.35% simple and on the line) and abstract (more than 67.80% simple) use different quantities: Theorem 1.3 (simple and on the line) and Corollary 1.2 (simple anywhere in the strip). The title and abstract phrasing invites confusion.

The Johns headline constant 0.9322 matches a number a search summary attributes to Sono (Bull. Aust. Math. Soc. 2016) as a GRH-conditional bound for low-lying zeros of primitive Dirichlet L-functions. This is a different quantity by the summaries, and I did not open Sono's paper, so this is an unverified coincidence to be checked.
Blinovsky's arXiv:1703.03827 claims RH only at v1 (2017), claims RH, GRH and the Ramanujan tau-Dirichlet hypothesis by v12 (2019), and claims RH only again from v13 (25 Dec 2025).

Ryazanov's arXiv:1808.10774: the current listing is titled 'A proof of the Riemann hypothesis on zeros of ζ-function'; per search snippets, the HTML versions v6 and v9 are titled 'A disproof of the Riemann hypothesis'.

summary: Searches: 44 web searches (listed verbatim in search.queries), with primary sources opened wherever the host allowed, and about 60 page fetches: the Anthropic post; the arXiv abstracts and HTML for 2608.13637, 2609.02882, 2610.08965, 2608.16034, 2609.27808, 2607.14515, 2503.05269, 2506.16115, 2404.16003, 2602.03626, 1912.04058, 1905.09385, 1808.10774, 2006.12546, 2105.07422, 1802.09704 and 2103.09418, and the Blinovsky listing across v1, v12, v13 and v15 and the current version; the openai/math README, CONTENTS, history, overview.tex, the Lean docs for family 003 and the Lean README, plus the preprint folder listing; the anthropics/zeta-23-lean README; the nic410 repository README and its VERIFICATION page; the Zenodo record for Johns; the MSP and sciepub journal pages; the Cambridge Open Engage page for Abe; and the Wikipedia article. Verdict on the GRH: no accepted proof or disproof. The Wikipedia article (last edited 2 Oct 2026, the most recent version I could read) still lists the GRH as open, notes that the only proven cases are in the function-field setting, and mentions none of the 2026 results. Events that move a quantity named in the GRH: (a) unconditional proportions of zeros simple and on the line for each fixed primitive Dirichlet character (Alpöge and Furman, Theorem B, Aug 2026, 2/3 in windows (T, 2T), with o(1) errors) and for averaged families (Hua and Yang, Aug 2026, 0.6725 and 0.8362; Johns, Sep 2026, weighted family, 0.9322); (b) OpenAI's zero-free half-plane Re s > 7/8 (and 11/12 companion) for all Dirichlet L-functions and a uniform real-zero gap (Oct 2026), both unreviewed. The closer calls are these. A proportion of zeros on the line is a relaxation of GRH's all-zeros statement, so whether a lower bound on that proportion 'moves the quantity named' is for the judging pass; I have recorded the windowing and the per-character versus averaged scope in each event. A zero-free region at 7/8 is a statement about where zeros are, not whether they lie on the line; I have recorded it as partial with no direction on the line. The real-zero exclusion (OpenAI, uniform gap) removes only zeros with 1 − β < c/log q, leaving 1/2 < β ≤ 1 − c/log q open. AI involvement in the Dirichlet-specific results: Alpöge and Furman's paper credits Claude with discovering the argument (its authors' own account, arXiv comments and title footnote; Anthropic's post gives the process and compute). Johns credits Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 agents with the mathematics, proofs, certificates and Lean work, with AI referees and no named human line-by-line check (Zenodo and VERIFICATION page). The OpenAI family 003 is credited to 'an unreleased internal OpenAI model' by the README. Knausgård's zeta paper describes itself as 'an experiment in AI-assisted mathematical research' and names only Claude, credited with an earlier argument it builds on. Hua–Yang, Lamzouri, Sono, Wu and the conditional papers show no AI system in what I read. Lamzouri's formal certificate for Proposition 2.1 is machine-generated (AxiomProver) but formalises a human-written argument, so it is recorded in the summary of his event and not in ai.systems. Two items were not used. The emergentmind page is a machine-generated summary and attributes a section to 'GPT-6 Astra Medium'; I did not rely on that name, which no primary source I opened gives. The Johns VERIFICATION page names 'Astra' as a reviewer, and I have recorded that name as the page gives it. Unverified or unopened: Zhang's Preprints.org record (blocked, 403; snippet-level dates), the Agélas HAL record (blocked, 403; described only through Brent's abstract), Sghiar's AI-assisted RH claim (ResearchGate, blocked; title only, not recorded as an event). Not recorded for lack of an opened source: Palojärvi–Simonič (arXiv:2410.22711, conditional on GRH), Thorner–Zhao (January 2026, automorphic L-functions, parent-level), Ray (arXiv:2511.06109, expository re-proof of Wu's result), Garunkštis–Paliulionytė (2025) and Sono's 2016 BAMS paper (both snippet-level). competing_reading: Reading the Dirichlet results as progress on the GRH: each fixed-character theorem (Alpöge–Furman Theorem B, 2/3 of zeros in windows simple and on the line) and each family average (Hua–Yang, Johns) is a quantitative move on the one thing the statement is about, which is where the zeros of Dirichlet L-functions lie. Reading them as settling nothing about the GRH: the statement is an all-zeros assertion, every result here is a lower bound on a proportion that is not one, the bounds are restricted to windows or to averages, and the simple-zero condition is a different property from location. The zero-free region at 7/8 and the Siegel gap are, on the strict reading, statements about where zeros are not, not about whether they lie on the line. The AI-attribution question is also open: the authors of 2608.13637 say the argument was 'discovered and written by Claude'; a reader who counts the authors as the originators would instead see two human-verified results and an AI-produced draft. The OpenAI release is less checked than the Anthropic one (no named human reading, Lean only in part, and an explicit warning that unformalised results 'could have issues').
what_would_settle_it: (1) For the proportion results: a formal statement and a Lean check of Theorem B (the Dirichlet extension) in the anthropics/zeta-23-lean project or a sibling repository, and an independent human reading of Theorem B. (2) For Johns' weighted-family result: a human line-by-line check, which the page says has not yet happened, and the Lean scope for Theorems 1.2 to 1.4(c), which are not formalised. (3) For OpenAI family 003: the statements of the lead paper and companion read from the PDFs (not parsed here), a Lean check that the formal statements match the informal ones, a resolution of the 7/8 versus 11/12 assignment, and the procedure used for 003 (the README's 'zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function' exception). (4) For the Siegel gap: the exact quantifiers in the PDF and whether c is effective. (5) For the Agélas claim: the body of the proof and Brent's Lemma 2.3 counterexample checked against it. (6) For Zhang and Blinovsky: a referee or expert reading of the GRH argument (Zhang's text was blocked; Blinovsky's GRH-carrying version between v2 and v12 is not located). (7) For the Johns 0.9322 coincidence: Sono (2016) read directly to compare its quantity with Johns' weighted statement.
